Probing chess based World Models

Code

1 Introduction

A world model represents the state of an environment and predicts how it will change in response to an action. I chose chess because I can reconstruct that state after every move and check whether the model has kept track of the pieces. Grandmasters of similar strength can look at that same position and still express their own styles through the moves they prefer, whether they choose to attack, defend, or play for control of the centre. I can train a probe to predict the contents of each square from a chess model’s internal activity, then reuse the same probe on models trained on data from specific grandmasters.

  • RQ1. When fine-tuning changes the world model’s policy, how accurately can the original probe still read the board?
  • RQ2. How similarly do the different world models represent the board position, and is there a way to map one representation to another?

2 Models and controls

I started with Karvonen’s 25-million-parameter chess model, pretrained on about 16 million Lichess games. I fine-tuned four copies, one on each grandmaster’s own moves. For Anatoly Karpov and Garry Kasparov, I used games played in person. For Magnus Carlsen and Andrew Tang, I used online bullet games with one minute per player. Within each pair, I matched the amount of move text used for training and chose checkpoints on validation games.

Karpov and Kasparov started with 2,103 and 1,024 games before splitting the data and matching training budgets. The bullet specialists trained on about six times as many games. KL measures how far each specialist’s next-character predictions shifted from the base, in nats per target character.

Did the choice of player change the moves? I compared the base and all four specialists on the same 1,500 positions. Within each pair, specialists trained on different players chose different moves about 14% of the time, versus 3–6.5% for two runs trained on the same player. Stockfish helped distinguish a stronger move from a preference between similarly good ones.

What was the probe reading? For each pair, I trained a probe on layer 6 of the base model and froze it. From move 16, I scored only occupied squares, where the probe had to identify the piece and its colour. On the in-person validation games, it misread 12% of those squares. A probe trained the same way on an untrained model misread 85%.

To check that the test could detect a wrong board, I replaced the internal activity for 5% of validation positions with activity from another game at the same move number. Error rose by 3.5 percentage points in both pairs, well above my preset tolerance of one point.

3 What changed in the first experiment

RQ1. How accurately the frozen probe read the board after fine-tuning

Each copy predicted its own player better, including in reserved head-to-head games and across seeds. The advantage was larger for Carlsen–Tang, primarily because of all the data. Across all four specialists, the frozen probe made at most one extra error per hundred occupied squares compared with the base model. Karpov was closest to the limit, rising from 12.14% to 13.00% error (+0.86 points, 95% interval +0.79 to +0.94).

The top choice changed on roughly one board in six. To isolate move quality, I took the 380 boards with at least two legal moves but only one within half a pawn of Stockfish’s best. The base found 244/380 (64.2%). Every copy corrected some base misses and introduced others. All four paired 95% intervals for the net change included zero when I resampled by game. In a second example of the base’s existing skill, it matched Kasparov against Spassky on move 27 by moving the knight from F3 to G5. Stockfish put the next-best move 1.11 pawns behind. The Kasparov copy preferred moving the other knight from C3 to E4. Annotated game

Four positions where the specialist found a better move

I selected one position from each player’s held-out games where the specialist and its second seed both picked Stockfish’s best move and the base chose another. I rechecked the best move among all legal moves at depth 18, then compared the two policies’ choices at that depth. Blue shows the specialist’s top move and orange the base’s. Evaluations are in pawns from the moving side’s perspective. The neutral-board table above gives the overall rate.

Karpov copy — defend before giving check. Against Nigel Short in 1992, the base wanted Black to move the knight to H4 and give check on move 43. White could take it with the pawn from G3. The specialist preferred moving the knight to H6, saving it and defending F7. Black was still worse, but its evaluation improved from −5.40 to −3.03. Short–Karpov game score

Kasparov copy — trade queens on the right square. Against Short in 1989, the base preferred moving Black’s queen from B5 to D7 on move 29, allowing White’s queen to take it there. The specialist preferred taking White’s queen on A4. White recaptured on A4 with the pawn from B3. Black then took the knight on F4 with the pawn from G5. The candidate moves evaluated to −1.94 and +2.55. The base itself gave that last pawn capture a 94.7% probability. All four specialists also ranked it first. Short–Kasparov game score

Carlsen copy — keep the position level. With White against Sergei Zhigalko, the base wanted to take Black’s rook on C2 with White’s rook on move 46. Black’s queen could take White’s rook on C2 with check and keep checking the exposed king. The specialist preferred taking the pawn on D5 with White’s queen, leaving White’s rook on F2. Stockfish evaluated the base’s choice at −2.30 and the specialist’s at 0.00. Replay from move 46

Tang copy — take the same rook with a different piece. With Black against Zhigalko, the base preferred taking White’s rook on E3 with Black’s rook on move 33. White could then move the queen to F7 with check, force Black’s king to H8, and move the queen to G8 for checkmate. The specialist preferred taking the same rook with Black’s queen. That leaves Black’s rook on E7, ready to take White’s queen if it comes to F7. Stockfish gave Black +4.64 after the queen capture. Replay from move 33

Which differences look like playing style

The four cases above measure move quality. To examine style, I selected different boards where both candidate moves were within half a pawn of Stockfish’s best. Both seeds of each specialist repeated its choice. A player’s own description provides context. The measured probability change tells us what the copy learned.

Karpov described a preference for active positional play in endings. Against Christiansen, the base preferred taking the pawn on C4 with Black’s rook on move 48. Fine-tuning raised the probability of moving the king to G5 from 28.8% to 39.1%, making the active king move its first choice. The engine scored both moves level. Across neutral boards, the Karpov copy gave king moves 0.48 percentage points more probability than the base. Karpov interview · Game score

Kasparov described himself as an attacking player. Against Shirov on move 31, the base preferred pushing the pawn to G6. The copy narrowly favored moving the queen to G6 to give check, chiefly because the probability of the pawn push fell from 28.3% to 21.0%. The engine put the two moves just 0.06 pawns apart. Across neutral boards, however, the Kasparov copy gave checks 0.79 percentage points less probability than the base. This particular check fits the description better than a general claim about checking frequency does. Kasparov interview

Carlsen said he chooses an attack, a defense or an ending according to the position. Against Tang, the base narrowly preferred moving Black’s bishop to H6 to give check on move 21. The Carlsen copy preferred taking White’s bishop on D4 with that same bishop, exchanging bishops. Its probability of the capture rose from 35.9% to 47.4%. The moves were just 0.03 pawns apart. Across neutral boards its capture probability stayed within 0.3 points of the base, so the shift here is specific to the position. Carlsen interview · Replay

Tang described his over-the-board style as versatile and credited positional training with broadening his early tactical game. In this bullet position against Carlsen, both policies answered a knight check on move 20 by taking the knight on F3 with White’s queen. The base already favored that recapture at 66.5%. Tang’s copy kept it first at 54.7% while giving more weight to taking the same knight with the pawn from G2. The moves were 0.19 pawns apart. Here the policy drifted while its first choice stayed the same. Tang interview · Replay

Where the specialist helped. Tang’s copy captured a rook with its queen. The base used its rook instead and allowed mate in two. Depth-18 Stockfish confirmed all four featured specialist moves.

From one move to a different game. Karpov and Kasparov copies disagreed on 14.2% of the neutral boards, versus 6.1–6.5% across seeds for one player. For Carlsen and Tang the rates were 14.6% versus 3.0–3.5%. Against the same base-model opponent from 600 shared starts, only 32% and 29% of eligible sequences, respectively, still matched after ten of the copies’ own moves. In one middlegame, the Karpov and Carlsen copies used White’s bishop to take Black’s bishop on E7. Black’s rook recaptured there, and White moved its remaining bishop to D3. The Kasparov and Tang copies moved a bishop to D3 first. Black’s bishop took White’s other bishop on G5, and White’s queen recaptured on G5. The engine separated the first moves by just 0.12 pawns.

RQ2. How closely the specialists’ board representations matched

On the same boards, each specialist’s layer-6 activity shifted by about 12% of its original length (median). Positions that were close together in the base model tended to stay close in each copy (rank correlation ≈ 0.99). Refitting the probe reduced Karpov’s extra error from 0.86 to 0.22 points and Kasparov’s from 0.52 to 0.10.

I fitted a rotation from each specialist back to the base model using paired positions, then tested the frozen probe on separate games. For Karpov, the rotation cut the extra error on occupied squares from 0.86 to 0.29 percentage points. For Kasparov, it fell from 0.52 to 0.01. Carlsen’s score barely changed, while Tang’s went from 0.01 points below the base error to 0.41 above it. Alignment helped most where the original probe had lost accuracy.

I pushed the internal signal for a movable white piece toward “empty” on 400 positions per pair. At medium strength, probability assigned to that piece’s legal moves fell 18.5% for Karpov, 17.2% for Kasparov, 10.2% for Carlsen and 9.5% for Tang, close to the respective base-model drops of 18.7% and 10.3%. Random edits of the same size changed it by less than 1%. The board signal remained readable and continued to influence moves.

4 Testing the frozen probe across Elo levels

All four specialists learned from grandmasters, and the copies in each pair chose the same move on about 86% of boards. My hunch is that players of similar strength often see the same strong moves. Across a wider range of Elo ratings, I’d expect differences in playing style and blunder rates to show up more clearly in the moves the models choose.

With another week, I’d fine-tune copies of the same base model on games from low, intermediate and high rating bands at one time control. Pooling games within each band could give me roughly ten times as much training data per copy. I’d match the training budgets and compare the copies on the same 1,500 held-out boards. If their move choices diverge more, I’d test whether the original frozen probe still reads the board within one extra error per hundred occupied squares relative to the base model. A consistent increase beyond that limit would change my conclusion.

5 What I would work on with Physical Reasoning

What excites me about probing a world model’s latent space is that it could show us what to teach it next. If a chess model loses track of pieces after exchanges, I’d use that finding to build training examples and test whether it learns to track the board more accurately and play stronger moves in new games.

I used AI to write code, analyze move choices, and prepare the diagrams.
